opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how the system is built. In the U.S., from a very young age, kids are asked to do "show and tell." You bring something from home, you stand in front of the class, and you explain why it matters to you. It sounds small, but it trains a habit: what you think is only real to other people once you've said it out loud, clearly, in a way they can follow.

When I first encountered this, my instinct was a bit skeptical. Where I grew up, there's this idea that the work should speak for itself, that if you're good, people will eventually notice, and that talking too much about yourself is a little vulgar. Modesty is a virtue. So at first the American style felt like self-promotion, maybe even a performance.

Over time I came to see it differently. In a society that's very large, very mobile, and very diverse, people don't share the same background or the same networks. Nobody knows your family, your teacher, your hometown. So the burden is on you to translate yourself, to make your value legible to strangers. Expression isn't just vanity; it's a kind of infrastructure. It's how trust gets built quickly between people who have no prior reason to trust each other.

There's also a deeper cultural layer, this belief that the individual is the basic unit, and that your perspective is worth hearing simply because it's yours. Classrooms reward participation, not just correct answers. Meetings expect you to push back. Silence is often read not as humility but as having nothing to contribute.

That said, I don't think it's purely good. It can reward people who are fluent talkers over people who are deep thinkers, and there's a real cost to that. I think the healthiest version is when expression is in service of substance: you do the hard thinking first, and then you take responsibility for communicating it well. For me, learning to do that was less about becoming louder and more about realizing that sharing what I see is part of the work, not separate from it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to understand is that it isn't really about confidence or personality. It's structural. In the U.S., the person evaluating you usually doesn't know you, doesn't know your school, doesn't know your family, and won't spend three years watching you quietly do good work before forming an opinion. So expression becomes the only channel through which your substance can reach other people. If you don't present it, functionally it doesn't exist.

When I first got there, I misread this. I thought people who talked a lot in meetings were performing, and that if I just did the work well, it would speak for itself. That's a very East Asian assumption, that quality is self-evident and modesty is a signal of depth. In the American context, silence isn't read as depth. It's read as absence. Nobody is being malicious about it, they just have no information.

The second layer is that Americans treat self-presentation as a form of responsibility toward other people, not just toward yourself. If you have a view and you don't share it, you've withheld something the group needed. So "speaking up" gets framed almost morally. I found that genuinely different from how I was raised, where speaking too early could be seen as taking up space you hadn't earned yet.

That said, I don't think the American version is simply better. It rewards a specific kind of fluency, and it can confuse articulateness with judgment. I've seen plenty of rooms where the most polished speaker was wrong and the person who actually understood the problem was sitting there deciding whether it was their place to interrupt. The system does lose something there.

Where I've landed personally is that expression is a skill, not an identity. You can learn to state your position clearly and early without becoming a different person. And the people I admire most in the U.S. aren't the loudest. They're the ones who say one precise thing at the right moment. That's actually not so far from what I grew up thinking a good person looked like. It just requires you to open your mouth.

astra-6.text:
I think in the U.S., expressing yourself is often seen as part of taking responsibility for your own opportunities. You’re expected to tell people what you think, what you’re good at, and what you want, rather than assume they’ll notice on their own.

That can be empowering. It gives you permission to have a voice, even when your perspective is different. But it can also create pressure: being good at something and being good at presenting yourself are two different abilities, and sometimes the second gets rewarded more than the first.

So I’d distinguish between making yourself understood and constantly trying to impress people. You can learn to communicate your strengths clearly without exaggerating them or becoming the loudest person in the room. And ideally, a society that values expression should also value listening—including listening to people who need a little more time to speak.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it reflects how much American society values individual agency. You’re often expected to explain who you are, what you think, and what you can contribute, rather than wait for someone else to recognize it. Presenting yourself becomes a way of helping people understand you.

That can be empowering, especially if you’re comfortable speaking up. But it can also create pressure: being good at expressing your abilities isn’t necessarily the same as having those abilities. Someone who’s quieter may have a great deal to offer and still be overlooked.

So I see value in learning to express yourself clearly, while also leaving room for different personalities. You should be able to make yourself heard without feeling that you have to perform all the time.
